title: Git for US Legislation (lexifina.com)
comments: I hadn't thought of using git to track the changes in legislation. This is a cool idea.In Australia, I spent a bit of time trying to work out how to find which politician voted for what (both at state and federal level), so that when elections come, you can single out the individuals who voted for what legislation. I think AI may make this easier, but the challenge is in not spamming the "free and open" access to the online record of our legislation.So far, it's probably a one-person $50K per year job to do this task manually, and the language of the public legislation record didn't lend itself easily to determining the laws or rights that actually changed when bills were passed into legislation. They are explicitly stated, but hard to distill with regexes, filters or other analysis tools (e.g. "Who voted to stop electric scooters going over 25km/h?") If you try reading the legislation, you will know what I mean."A complete and open record of the proceedings of our parliament" still needs people spend a good chunk of time interpreting and summarising it (e.g. the media, commentators, etc) which means it's a time-consuming hobby or a paid gig.reply

title: Ghostty 1.4 (ghostty.org)
comments: These are Ghostty GUI release notes, but I want to take a moment to highlight the libghostty progress we've made since Ghostty 1.3.As a reminder, libghostty is the highly portable, embeddable library that provides core terminal emulation, render state, and more. I always felt that a free, high qualty, lightweight, reusable terminal emulation core would benefit the developer world more than any single GUI application. And that is playing out!It is and always was my true purpose with the Ghostty project (I said this in my first ever talk about Ghostty!). I've jokingly said many times that Ghostty GUI is just a glorified tech demo for libghostty. That's not fair though, because GUI is great and there are really talented people working on it.Since I started the project, Ghostty has always gotten people saying "I don't understand why you'd start a terminal emulator today." Well, the answer is libghostty. It's truly unique and its enabling something special (imo!).Highlights of libghostty since 6 months ago (none of the below was true 6 months ago):- Libghostty has nearly 100% coverage of all of Ghostty's core (and you can compile with flags to remove any of these features for size/safety): https://libghostty.tip.ghostty.org/- Libghostty now builds and is tested (in CI) for: Apple (macOS, iOS, visionOS), Windows (MSVC and GNU), Linux, FreeBSD, Android, WebAssembly, and freestanding (i.e. direct on hardware with no OS).- Libghostty has bindings in pretty much every popular programming language: C, Zig, Go, Swift, Python, Rust, .NET, etc.- Libghostty's memory requirements have dramatically shrunk to enable the portability above. There's still work to do but a single empty terminal now takes 90% less memory. And at scale I've proven 10,000 active (input/output happening) terminals on a Linux server with 4 cores and 8 GB of RAM.- Libghostty powers all JetBrains IDE terminals, over 12.5 million active users. https://blog.jetbrains.com/platform/2026/10/jetbrains-termin...- Libghostty is the most popular core behind the wave of venture-backed "agentic" terminals and editors, such as Herdr, cmux, and many others.- Libghostty is being discussed and has been verbally accepted to replace the terminal core in Neovim: https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/39773 (work still to be done)- Libghostty powers a really popular and powerful terminal emulator for emacs (Ghostel): https://github.com/dakra/ghostel- Libghostty's speed is used by Antithesis to fuzz popular terminal programs and has directly led to hundreds of bug fixes sent upstream to programs such as tmux, btop, shells, and other terminal emulators. :)- And so much more: https://github.com/Uzaaft/awesome-libghosttyLibghostty is really successfully turning into the tide that raises all boats. As it becomes more popular, Ghostty itself gets more performant and stable, and so does everyone else. It is also a vehicle for delivering modern terminal emulation to the widest source possible.I plan on tagging libghostty 1.0 in the next few months and declaring ABI stability at that point!reply

title: Survival LLM: AI assistant and emergency library that runs on your own computer (brangus.io)
comments: This topic is bringing out the hallucination-panic crowd.It's perfectly safe to use LLMs to surface underlying data and knowledge without having to trust that it's giving you correct advice.Use the LLM as search technology: string match -> semantic search -> search intelligence.This is especially helpful when you don't know the right question to ask. Semantics only help you find text that is semantically near the input query. Semantics won't help you when what you are looking for is connected to what you have by something other than semantics, like causation, mechanism, or interpretation.Trying to figure out why your crops aren't growing well will likely require you to read several articles across a range of sciences, probably scoped to the specific conditions you are dealing with. A semantic search is not going to surface those first.Allowing an LLM to chain together several sources for you to read first does not require you to ask it for a conclusion.reply

The readme on Github does say the system produces hallucinated sources https://github.com/anonnerdfrenzy/survival-llm#how-the-model..., but really you're correct, for this kind of highly targeted use case the LLM's summary could probably be ignored entirely and the system could work extremely well even just as a search engine: index all of the content up front, chunked by paragraph and maybe enriched with a HyDE step, have the LLM facilitate running a handful of hybrid keyword/semantic searches based on the user's question and reranking the results, and show the exact pieces of text in the corpus that are most responsive to their question. No summary needed.reply

A great strength of LLMs is how they provide useful answers even if the prompt has glaring spelling or grammatical mistakes. If your prompt is not great, as you said, they will reply in a way that helps you identify that flaws, and learn how to steer the model better.They're amazingly useful tools, but they're nowhere the level believers want them to be, not yet.reply

title: Python's experimental JIT to be removed (lwn.net)
comments: Unfortunate. I've been following the work on it occasionally.On one hand, it seemed like JIT work was really progressing in high gear until SC requested a new PEP. Also unfortunate, as it seemed like part of the hope for the JIT was that it'd counter the performance penalty from free threading.On the other, it did feel (to me) like with all the fancy (and definitely cool) optimizations it got (automatic refcount operation removal, new type-based specializations, inplace math operations), the macrobenchmark benefits weren't _that_ exciting for a JIT. It definitely has potential for more, maybe with even fancier optimizations like unboxing ints, but the complexity just keeps going up.> It said that the PEP was "overly optimistic" about user-visible differences with the JIT enabled.The JIT is technically generated from the same source as the interpreter loop itself, so originally the differences were extremely unlikely, but I imagine the risk just kept going up as new JIT-only paths and optimizations were introduced.And politically, I feel like SC’s reasoning was just “this side project has landed in main branch almost by accident and has been stewing without oversight ever since, with no stabilization in sight”; and the latest PEP was probably still too vague, with a lot of “here’s more things we can add to the stew” - so I can understand if SC wasn’t satisfied.reply

I think this is a major issue with requiring a PEP for what's a performance optimization.JITs are big nasty things that by their nature have to do a lot of things.  You are basically saying "Give us a PEP for a new python interpreter and compiler".What they do is fuzzy by their nature because optimizations are very rarely universally beneficial.  It's a game of measuring, looking for regressions, and tackling the biggest problem next for whatever sample applications you have available.  You always run into the risk of overfitting on top of all that (You may have made django faster, but you've made flask slower).This is the sort of thing that, IMO, should not go through the PEP process.  It's an implementation detail for the runtime.Imagine, for example, if the JVM needed a bunch of JEPs for JIT improvements.  They'd never get done.  Or if any javascript engine needed ECMA acceptance before they could do a new JIT optimization.reply

> Imagine, for example, if the JVM needed a bunch of JEPs for JIT improvements.They do:https://openjdk.org/jeps/197https://openjdk.org/jeps/515Not every optimization requires a JEP, but certainly something as big as "add or remove a JIT" would 100% require a JEP.reply

> Imagine, for example, if the JVM needed a bunch of JEPs for JIT improvements.FWIW, I definitely can find a bunch of both PEPs and JEPs for internal optimizations, random examples:https://peps.python.org/pep-0509/https://openjdk.org/jeps/147reply

You can find those JEPs, but frankly they are there for 1 of 2 reasons.1. An outsider to the regular OpenJDK dev team proposing an optimization.2. Advertising for a cool new performance tweak with potentially large impact.You'll also notice that the JEP descriptions are very different from PEP descriptions.Probably the largest JEP for the JVM, Valhallahttps://openjdk.org/jeps/401Does not have the same level of requirements being asked of the Python JIT.  Further, it's well understood that this JEP will "live on main" for quite some time in preview before it's accepted and merged.What the JEP does, instead, is simply describe the feature and potential risks.The vast majority of JVM optimizations do not get a JEP.reply

Fair, I don’t argue with that, I’m not knowledgeable about Java’s processes. Just one thing:> The vast majority of JVM optimizations do not get a JEP.In Python too. Still, the JIT really is just a really big thing. I don’t know if there could be a better way to do it, as either 1. You develop it off-branch and… make an enormous PR when you’re done, with risks of getting rejected anyway? Or 2, you allow more experiments on main like Rust, but then you end up with hundreds of minor half-maintained nightly-only features, possibly conflicting with each other, and eventually go through bureaucracy to remove them anyway.reply

So, I'd grant that it'd probably be a JEP for java (the initial JIT) but not that every change to the JIT would result in a new JEP.  Java's JIT, hotspot, was integrated right before they started the JEP process.  The JEP for the JIT would likely be pretty boring like "It's a JIT, it does this, in some applications we see this sort of speed up".  Much like the AOT JEP https://openjdk.org/jeps/514The Java governance allows for a lot more open ended projects with follow ups.  Not that it's reckless, Valhalla is proof of that, but rather that once something is good enough they are pretty open to just shipping it as a preview feature and refining until it is worthy of being stable.That's why, for example, we saw ZGC get merged, and then JDK after JDK seeing continuing development and improvement on ZGC (Or G1 for that matter).  These GCs were fairly rough on their first release and now they are pretty much best in class.I see a Python JIT as the same thing.  Delivering the infrastructure for a JIT would need a PIP, but I wouldn't put in things like "acceptance criteria" beyond "doesn't break older code".  I would expect such a project to get continual updates without PEPs.reply

>  I would expect such a project to get continual updates without PEPs.Just for completeness: the original JIT PR was merged quite enthusiastically 
and only after the fact it was pointed out that it should have went through a PEP process [1]. The following PEP 744 was of the “informational” type, and the just-withdrawn PEP 836 was the first “standards track” PEP, which means that (in my understanding) it’s technically the first actual PEP that the SC would formally comment on. So in a way it’s not “can we update the JIT” PEP, but the first real “does SC want this JIT as proposed” PEP.That said, I do agree with most of what you said, especially the acceptance criteria part.The issue I have and find it hard to resolve is that since the code was already on main, the feature was already in “sunk cost” mode. It’s hard when the code is already on main and another 3 optimization PRs are always there behind the corner, but it needs to be possible for SC to say “we decided it’s not actually worth all this complexity for <some small number>% speed improvement” (I’m not commenting whether in this particular case it’d have been a right call), and the PEP (if not withdrawn) was the way to exercise that control.[1] https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/113465#issuecomment-1...reply

The original JIT certainly did not get a JEP, because JEPs replaced the previous JSR process.And even then, Hotspot did not got a JSR, because all that work was done before Sun started collaborating with industry partners for Java evolution.They "simply" ported the JIT compiler from the Strongtalk acquisition into Java.reply

> On the other, it did feel (to me) like with all the fancy (and definitely cool) optimizations it got (automatic refcount operation removal, new type-based specializations, inplace math operations), the macrobenchmark benefits weren't _that_ exciting for a JIT. It definitely has potential for more, maybe with even fancier optimizations like unboxing ints, but the complexity just keeps going up.Zero chance of shoehorning that into a standards-compliant Python runtime. Some things are too fundamental to change without affecting the user-visible language: JITting, lazy imports, threading, copying gc, ref counting, etc.reply

title: Classification of Finite Simple Groups Formalized in Lean (axiommath.ai)
comments: Out of curiosity: is it possible to take a frontier model and just let it loose on all math textbooks out there, converting each and every proof/theorem/lemma/etc. into Lean? A frontier model should be able to do that, right? And it's a one-time task: do it once and it's there for eternity, available as a library to be used in other proofs.Maybe my understanding of Lean is wrong; I'm thinking of it as a programming language but for Math.reply

Axiom MTS here. What you describe is pretty close to how we formalised this proof, which is scattered across more than 500 articles and books: a swarm of agents was tasked with going through all these sources.One challenge is assembling everything into a coherent whole, since the same informal concept can be formalised in slightly different but incompatible ways.reply
What were the agents based on?reply
[flagged]
Producing a formalized proof from a non-formalized proof in a paper or book should not be considered a violation of copyright.reply
Indeed; one cannot copyright mathematical ideas, only their specific expressions.  And the formalization is a different expression.reply

Yes, but thing is, for a lot of basic stuff there are myriad ways in which it is formulated, so humans have to decide which of them goes in the library. Of course you can include two or five or ten equivalent formulations (like textbooks sometimes do) but still, not everything under the sun.Probably this will be done in some form in the coming months.reply

The really interesting aspect of this, IMHO, is discovering what theorem formulations combine together well as a whole. It's much akin to a software architecture problem.Metamath has done quite a bit or primary research into this. Theorems often have a slightly non-standard, but more general form.One can ask things like, "what is the equivalent of functional programming?" Or, "is there global state?" It's a perspective on reverse mathematics.reply

> Of course you can include two or five or ten equivalent formulations (like textbooks sometimes do) but still, not everything under the sun.Note that mathlib currently includes duplicates of many theorems; I believe deduplication is an active goal (if not one seeing much labor right now).reply
Yes and no. With enough compute, probably, but doing this does not necessarily yield a reusable library. See https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/10/16/how-to-formaliz...reply
